Forensics: the target's exact flag-section signature (lbu 5 / sb 5 / lui 4, three addend-0 bases, four surviving reloads) is reachable in NON-VOLATILE C via a cse basic-block boundary — refuting the s

frontier.hypothesis: There is a C construct that puts a CODE_LABEL surviving cse2 between the flag blocks at ZERO instruction cost — and it is the whole remaining gap, because p1 shows a surviving boundary already produces the target's exact access/address signature.
frontier.mechanism: cse_end_of_basic_block (cse.c:8039) stops at a CODE_LABEL in both passes, but the follow_jumps / skip_blocks extension at cse.c:8102-8184 walks straight through a conditional branch whose target label has LABEL_NUSES == 1 — which is true of all three of this function's if-join labels, so today they are NOT boundaries. A label with NUSES != 1 ends the block. The cost of every boundary measured so far (one-iteration for: 9 insns; real loop: collapses the unrolled shape) comes from the branch that creates the second use, so the question is whether a second LABEL_REF can exist without a new branch — e.g. a shared end label reached from two arms that the target's own branch structure already contains, a switch, or an if/else whose join is also a goto target.
frontier.next_probe: Read cse.c:8102-8184 for the exact extension conditions, then enumerate C control-flow shapes whose RTL gives a join label LABEL_NUSES >= 2 between the flag blocks: the shared-end-label technique (.claude/rules/shared-end-label.md), if/else with a common tail, a two-arm goto to one label, and a switch over the bit index. Score each honestly and read greg/jump2 to confirm the label survives into the final code. Check LABEL_NUSES directly in the jump.fn dumps rather than inferring it. structural or rederive modality.

frontier.hypothesis: Even with a free boundary between the flag blocks, the target's FIRST reload (lbu a0,0(v1) at insn 13, immediately after sb a0,0(v1) at insn 11, with no label, call or store between them) needs its own explanation — it is the only pair the boundary model cannot cover from the target's own instruction stream.
frontier.mechanism: The &0xF8 read-modify-write and block 1's read share base $v1 with nothing between them, so at cse time either a boundary existed there and was erased by a later pass without residue (only possible if the branch creating it became provably dead — a forbidden dead-branch construct), or the mem was not recordable (volatile, cse.c:7329, which s3 ruled out on policy), or the two accesses had different address rtxs that were later allocated the same hard register (impossible: each rtx needs its own materialisation).
frontier.next_probe: Take the p1 dump and check what jump2 / flow do to a boundary label whose branch is later removed; separately, enumerate the passes after cse2 that can delete a CODE_LABEL plus its branch with zero residue and test whether any is reachable without a constant condition. If none is, this sub-question — not the reload question — becomes the escalation's core. forensics modality.

frontier.hypothesis: The F3 escalation packet is NOT ready to file and its premise is now known to be wrong; do not file it from a non-escalation modality.
frontier.mechanism: s3-H4/s6 asserted an impossibility that s7 refuted by measurement (p1). The two remaining sanctioned axes named by s6's frontier are now measured dead, but s7 opened a NEW, cheap, honest axis (zero-cost cse2-surviving label boundaries) that has never been probed at all, so the function is still plainly grindable.
frontier.next_probe: Do NOT file. Work frontier item 1 first. If and only if the label-boundary family is exhausted should the packet be rewritten around the corrected claim: 'every cse2-surviving basic-block boundary construct costs instructions the target does not have', with p1's signature match as the central exhibit.
